# The degree ledger on the WIDENED adaptation: `deg D = n` over arbitrary affine pieces

The colength↔degree identity of `Picard/DivisorFamilyFieldDegree.lean`, ported from
`DivisorAdaptation` (pieces typed into a fixed pair of pinned `P¹` charts) to `AffAdaptation`
(arbitrary affine opens, human decision I-0492).  The port is **complete**: the widened
`deg_presentationDivisor_eq_finrank_glued` and its `deg = n` corollary are proved here, and
nothing in the chain remains conditional on the chart typing.

## What the port cost, measured rather than predicted

The board carried this as a **four**-lemma port.  It is five: the prescription omitted
`coeffAt_eq_toAdd_ordZ_eqn`, the coefficient dictionary that both other geometric lemmas call.
That is the only way the estimate was wrong, and it was wrong in the cheap direction — not one
proof step of any of the five differs from its chart-typed original.

Two substitutions carry the entire widening, and both replace a *derivation* by a structure
**field**:

* `DivisorAdaptation.isAffineOpen_pieces` is a two-case `rcases` on the `Sum` index proving each
  piece is a basic open of a pinned affine chart; `AffCoverData.isAffineOpen_pieces` is the field.
  The keystone that consumes it (`RiemannRoch/ChartColength.lean`'s
  `finrank_quotient_span_section`) takes `IsAffineOpen V` as an *argument* — it never wanted a
  chart.
* the three-line `relCover_sup` + `cover₀`/`cover₁` block inside the assembly produces exactly
  `∃ j, p.1 ∈ pieces j`; widened, that is `AffCoverData.exists_mem_pieces`, the joint covering
  field.

So the pinned pair was never load-bearing for the degree ledger.  It was the chart-typed **cost**
of two facts `AffCoverData` assumes, which is why an earlier pricing of this port as *obstructed*
by the covering was backwards (retracted at `Picard/DivisorFamilyAffAbel.lean`, issue I-1098).

* `AffAdaptation.gluedSubmodule_eq_top_of_separated`, `finrank_glued_eq_sum_of_separated` — the
  algebraic half: separation collapses the equalizer to the product, and Mayer–Vietoris finrank
  additivity with no overlap correction.
* `AffAdaptation.coeffAt_eq_toAdd_ordZ_eqn` — the coefficient dictionary (the fifth lemma).
* `AffAdaptation.finrank_colength_eq_sum` — the per-piece degree reading, on an arbitrary affine

* `AffAdaptation.deg_presentationDivisor_eq_finrank_glued` — the geometric half.
* `AffAdaptation.IsCertified.finrank_glued` — the field half.
* `AffAdaptation.deg_presentationDivisor_eq_of_isCertified` — `deg D = n`.
* `DivisorAdaptation.sep_toAff`, `exists_widened_deg_eq_of_certifiedFamily_sep` — the joint
  non-vacuity witness for the corollary's two hypotheses, at every `n`.

## What is NOT closed by this file

`hdegAff` (`Picard/DivisorFamilyAffAbel.lean`) is the *Abel-value* ledger — the widened Abel value
of a degree-`n` widened class has degree `n` at every field point — and it is still an explicit
hypothesis there.  This file supplies the identity that gate needed, not the gate: the remaining

divisor's degree through the field collapse to the Picard class.  Nothing here should be read as
discharging `rep` or any antecedent of the atlas assembly.

1	---
2	name: horizon
3	description: How to work inside an Archon Horizon workspace — orient from on-disk state, pick the highest-value formalization work, record progress as commits, and coordinate. Load this first; it points to the specialized skills for detail. Editable per workspace.
4	---
5	
6	You are working inside an **Archon Horizon** workspace: a place where AI agents
7	formalize mathematics in Lean 4 across one or more projects. This skill is the
8	map. It is deliberately short and **you can edit it** (it lives at
9	`.claude/skills/horizon/SKILL.md` in this workspace) — tune it to how you want to
10	work. It points to focused skills; load those on demand rather than up front.
11	
12	## You are a team; the workspace is where teams collaborate
13	
14	Think of your session as **one team**: you (the lead) plus the subagents you
15	spawn as your **workers**, with the tools and skills available to you. A
16	`horizon run` is your team working through its task. Other runs are **other
17	teams** working in parallel on the *same shared workspace* — one Lean project set,
18	one roadmap/board, one ledger, one inbox.
19	
20	You do not manage other teams and they do not manage you. You coordinate through
21	**shared state**, not meetings:
22	
23	- **The board (roadmap)** is the shared plan. Keep your items' status/owner/
24	  milestone current so other teams see what you hold and where it's going.
25	- **The inbox** is asynchronous messaging + memory across teams (skill:
26	  `horizon-inbox`): shared notes, per-task private items, and direct messages to
27	  another team.
28	- **Commits** are the durable record; reading recent ledger history tells you what
29	  other teams just produced (skill: `project-git`).
30	
31	Before you start, be aware of who else is live (see "Is another run live" below).
32	A short **synchronizer** digest is printed to stderr at the start of your CLI
33	commands. Its attention order is deliberate: `REQUIRED` active protections,
34	`ACTION` unread conversations, advisory unread inbox, then session/runtime and
35	other live runs. Read it; it is how you stay aware without asking anyone. A new
36	conversation or reply invalidates the digest cache immediately. If stderr is
37	redirected, the same protection/conversation lanes are the first `attention`
38	object in `horizon inbox list --json`.
39	
40	## Orient (pull state, don't assume it)
41	
42	**Start here:** your prompt says nothing about who ran before you. Usually
43	somebody did — often minutes ago, often on this same task, and their report was
44	written for you. Skill: `horizon-start` — one cheap pass that works out which
45	situation you were launched into (fresh run, hand-off from the session that just
46	finished, resume after a crash, or outside a run) and what to read for each.
47	
48	The workspace root is `$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT`; your shell may start in a member
49	project rather than at that root. The absolute path to this skill is
50	`$ARCHON_HORIZON_SKILL`. Live state is under
51	`$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT/.archon-horizon/` and the manifest is
52	`$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT/config.yaml`. Read what you need, when you need it — via the
53	`horizon` CLI (invoke it as `"$HORIZON_BIN" …`):
54	
55	- **Roadmap** — YOUR strategy sketch across *all* projects, kept as a nested
56	  outline. `"$HORIZON_BIN" roadmap list` renders the indented tree with per-parent
57	  progress (`active · 3/7 done`); `--focus <id>` shows one subtree, `--max-depth 0`
58	  the top level only. Structure it: nest sub-goals with `--parent`, keep your
59	  item's status/strategy current as you work. It doubles as the **project board**:
60	  set `--owner <team>` (who holds it), `--milestone <label>` (a free grouping tag,
61	  filter with `roadmap list --milestone <label>`), and pin concrete deliverables
62	  with `--pin-commit <sha>`. Roadmap commands print a **warning**
63	  when parent/child statuses disagree (all sub-items done but parent open, or a
64	  done parent with open children) — nothing is auto-corrected; you decide whether
65	  to fix it or leave it (it may be intentional). They also warn when too many
66	  milestones claim simultaneous `active` focus.
67	- **Tasks** — a specific piece of work, usually the one a human launched and is
68	  watching. `"$HORIZON_BIN" task …`. Task commands warn when the open queue grows
69	  beyond the advisory limit or a `running` status looks orphaned.
70	- **Inbox** — how teams talk across sessions and projects. Leave a note for the
71	  next session; read what past ones left. `"$HORIZON_BIN" inbox …` (skill:
72	  `horizon-inbox`). Items can be **owned by your task** (private, e.g. your team's
73	  memory) or **shared with everyone** (the default); read-state is per-team, so
74	  `inbox list --mine --unread` is your team's fresh queue, and you can
75	  direct-message another team with `--to task:<id>`. Inbox commands warn when the
76	  open working set—especially `memory` and `info`—needs review.
77	- **Inbox attention order** — before edits, inspect all open `protection` items
78	  (standing constraints, whether read or unread), then open unread
79	  `conversation` items and reply or mark them read. Other kinds are advisory
80	  context. In an agent session an unqualified `inbox list` defaults to open items
81	  and sorts in this order; use an explicit status to audit history.
82	- **Conversation discipline** — use a conversation only when a reply/decision is
83	  expected. Search and reuse an open thread before starting one. Its initiator is
84	  a participant and owns closure: after consuming the answer, add a concise
85	  conclusion if needed and archive the thread. Reply to human-started threads but
86	  leave their closure to the human unless asked otherwise (skill: `horizon-inbox`).
87	- **Blueprint graph** — declaration dependencies and what's proved. `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> …` (skill: `hgraph`).
88	  Each node is also an **hgraph** file with attached comments/reviews —
89	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> frontier` ranks what to prove next, and node-scoped failure memory
90	  goes on the node itself (skill: `hgraph`).
91	- **Memory** — durable facts/dead-ends live in the inbox: read with
92	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" inbox list --kind memory --json`, write with
93	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" inbox add --kind memory --to horizon --body …`.
94	- **Usage** — your token/cost consumption this session and run, budget headroom,
95	  and recent rate-limit signals: `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json`. See
96	  "Pace yourself" below for how to act on it.
97	
98	## Your session's identity (environment variables)
99	
100	The harness exports these to every session — read them instead of guessing:
101	
102	| Variable | Meaning |
103	|---|---|
104	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT` | workspace root (use for `--root`-free CLI calls) |
105	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_SKILL` | absolute path to this `SKILL.md` (never resolve it relative to the shell cwd) |
106	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_RUN` | run id (e.g. `0163`) |
107	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_SESSION` | this session's name (e.g. `0002-horizon-T-1`) |
108	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_SESSION_DIR` | this session's directory (transcript, usage.json, report) |
109	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUND` / `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUNDS` | which round this is (0-based) / the run's planned total |
110	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK` / `ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK_TITLE` | the task id / title (full body: `"$HORIZON_BIN" task show "$ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK" --json`) |
111	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_PROJECTS` | comma-separated projects this task spans |
112	| `HORIZON_BIN`, `HORIZON_GIT` | absolute paths to the CLI and the ledger-git wrapper |
113	| `HORIZON_LEDGER_GIT_DIR`, `HORIZON_LEDGER_WORK_TREE` | the workspace ledger repo + its work tree — `"$HORIZON_GIT" …` is shorthand for `git --git-dir "$HORIZON_LEDGER_GIT_DIR" --work-tree "$HORIZON_LEDGER_WORK_TREE" …` |
114	
115	## Pace yourself (usage & interruption risk)
116	
117	Sessions end for reasons you don't control: rate limits, usage caps, budgets.
118	The defense is NOT to avoid work — it is to make interruption cheap:
119	
120	- **Commit at every coherent point** (plain git into the ledger, below). If
121	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json` shows low budget headroom or recent
122	  `rate_limit`/`usage_limit` signals, commit what you have NOW and prefer
123	  finishing the piece in flight over opening a new front.
124	- If this is the run's **last round** (`ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUND` + 1 ==
125	  `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUNDS`), leave the workspace hand-off-clean: commit, update
126	  the roadmap/task status, and write the report as if nobody continues today.
127	- Interrupted anyway? Nothing is lost that was committed — the next session
128	  resumes from the ledger (see "Resuming" below).
129	
130	## One-shot discipline (important)
131	
132	This session runs to completion and is **not resumed** — you will not be re-invoked
133	when a background job finishes. So **run work in the foreground and block on it**
134	(builds, checks, subagents). Anything you leave running in the background, or leave
135	uncommitted, may be lost when the session ends. Commit early and often (below).
136	
137	## Pick the highest-value work
138	
139	Read the roadmap and the live Lean state, then commit to the most valuable next
140	piece. A node being large, multi-session, or blocked on missing mathlib
141	infrastructure is **not** a reason to skip it — start it, build the missing
142	lemma/definition yourself as project-local infrastructure, and push it as far as
143	you genuinely can. Prefer ambitious progress over defensive avoidance.
144	
145	If this session was launched on a specific task, make concrete progress on that
146	task's REAL objective — don't preemptively pivot to easy unrelated wins because
147	the objective is large. Leave a concise task comment only for a durable state
148	change or blocker, not every action. You own the task's terminal status (skill:
149	`task-status`): set `--status done` only when the objective is FULLY complete;
150	`blocked`/`failed` if genuinely stuck; set nothing if it's only partly advanced
151	(it returns to the queue).
152	
153	## Fresh-context checkpoints
154	
155	The old Ground pass is no longer a second orchestrator role, but independent
156	review is still part of convergence. Spawn the **`ground`** subagent at these
157	checkpoints:
158	
159	- before marking a multi-step task `done`;
160	- after every two substantive Horizon sessions on a long-running task;
161	- immediately after a strategy pivot, a broad workspace edit, or a surprising
162	  clean/build result.
163	
164	Give it the task/project scope and ask it to inspect the actual ledger diff,
165	blueprint graph, Lean state, roadmap, inbox, and reports with fresh context. It
166	is read-only on source and reports issues/memory; reconcile its findings before
167	continuing. Use **`work-reviewer`** for a narrow diff/proof audit and **`janitor`**
168	when the main concern is workspace hygiene. A one-session task may skip the
169	periodic checkpoint, but must still obtain a fresh-context review before a
170	terminal `done` claim.
171	
172	Schedule upkeep even when the last command did not print a warning. On a
173	multi-session run, dispatch **`janitor` at the start of every second Horizon
174	session** and before the final report; on a one-session task, dispatch it once
175	before claiming completion if the run touched roadmap, task, or inbox state.
176	Record the checkpoint in the report and wait for the helper before continuing.
177	If `janitor` is unavailable, ask **`ground`** for the same hygiene inspection;
178	Ground is read-only, so apply or explicitly record its findings yourself.
179	
180	## Warnings are work
181	
182	Commands report problems for a reason — never scroll past them. `lake build`
183	warnings, `horizon graph sync` warnings, roadmap consistency warnings, deprecation
184	notices from any tool: if your change caused it, **fix it now** (it is part of
185	the task); if it's pre-existing or caused by the tool/command itself, don't
186	silently ignore it — record it as a memory item, file an inbox `issue`, or
187	address it `--to human` when a human decision is needed. A warning that
188	survives your session should be one you *chose* to leave, with a trace saying
189	why.
190	
191	Collection-health warnings are a dispatch trigger, not background noise. When
192	`inbox`, `roadmap`, or `task` reports an overloaded queue, stale running item,
193	or status mismatch, pause the proof loop and spawn **`janitor`** with the
194	workspace scope. Wait for it, reconcile its report, rerun the command, and
195	record any warning that remains intentionally. Do this at most once for the
196	same warning in a session; a persistent warning still needs a report or inbox
197	issue rather than repeated no-op calls.
198	
199	## Do the work (Lean)
200	
201	For any Lean edit, load `lean-check` before touching the file and follow its
202	required LSP loop: query the target with `lean_diagnostic_messages` or
203	`lean_goal` before the first edit and after each subsequent edit. Keep `lake
204	build` for the final session boundary or a specifically required kernel check;
205	LSP is enough between edits and proof obligations. Use the narrowest `lake env
206	lean` fallback when LSP is unavailable, and do not duplicate that check when the
207	configured final build covers the same files.
208	
209	**Do not `grep` for a lemma.** Grep matches names you already guessed; it cannot
210	find the lemma whose name you don't know, and that is the one that costs you an
211	afternoon. This workspace indexes every declaration in every project *and* in
212	mathlib — query it:
213	
214	| You want | Use | Not |
215	|---|---|---|
216	| "does this lemma exist, anywhere?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" search "<words or name>" --json` | `grep -r` |
217	| "what's the lemma for this *statement*?" | LSP `lean_leansearch` (natural language) | guessing names |
218	| "what matches this *type*?" | LSP `lean_loogle` (`Nat → ?a → ?a`) | `grep` |
219	| "does something in scope close this goal?" | LSP `lean_local_search` / `lean_hover_info` | reading files |
220	| "what should I prove next?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> frontier` (ranked) | scanning the blueprint |
221	| "what does this node depend on / block?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> get label:<id>` | reading imports |
222	| "is the proof right?" | `lake env lean <file>` (narrowest faithful check) | `lean_diagnostic_messages` alone |
223	
224	`"$HORIZON_BIN" search` covers **your projects and mathlib together**, which is
225	its whole point: the premise you need is usually already in mathlib under a name
226	you would never have grepped for. One query costs a second; re-proving an
227	existing lemma costs a session. If it reports a library as unindexed, fix that
228	first (`lake build`, then `"$HORIZON_BIN" search --reindex`) rather than falling
229	back to grep.
230	
231	Grep is still the right tool for what it *is* good at: finding a known string, a
232	specific file, or every call site of a name you already have.
233	
234	- Search before proving — the lemma may already exist. Skill: `leansearch`.
235	- Use the **Lean LSP MCP** for tight proof feedback, then verify with the narrowest
236	  faithful `lake` / `lake env lean` check. Skill: `lean-check`.
237	- Use the DAG to choose and scope work, not just to report it. Skill: `hgraph`.
238	- When editing blueprint material, follow the house format. Skill: `blueprint-conventions`.
239	  The blueprint is timeless mathematics, never a formalization journal. Put Lean
240	  implementation notes, failed tactics, and declaration-specific progress on the
241	  corresponding hgraph node with `graph add comment`; do not insert
242	  "Formalization note" paragraphs into blueprint `.tex` files.
243	
244	## Read the other projects
245	
246	They are in this workspace for a reason: the same lemma, pattern, or dead end has
247	often already been worked out next door. `"$HORIZON_BIN" search` spans **all**
248	projects — an existing construction in another project is a lead, whether you
249	import it, copy the approach, or read its blueprint. `references/` holds the
250	original sources (skill: `references`). Staying inside your own project because
251	the task named it is how the workspace re-derives the same thing three times.
252	
253	## Delegating beyond your team (ask permission first)
254	
255	Your normal way to parallelize is **within** your team: spawn subagents/workers
256	(skill: `subagents`) and dispatch scoped work to them in the foreground. That
257	needs no permission.
258	
259	Launching work **outside** your team — creating new tasks for other teams, or
260	spawning a whole new `horizon run` — is different: it spends the user's compute
261	and accounts, so it is **off by default**. Before you even consider it, read the
262	standing consent: `"$HORIZON_BIN" permissions --json`. It reports
263	`allow_launch_tasks`, `allow_launch_runs`, `max_parallel_sessions`, any declared
264	`accounts`, and free-form notes the user left (e.g. which account to prefer, when
265	limits reset). If both `allow_*` are false (the default), **do not** create tasks
266	or launch runs on the user's behalf — instead leave an inbox item `--to human`
267	proposing the delegation and why. Only when a flag is enabled may you act within
268	its stated caps, and follow the account/usage notes the user recorded.
269	
270	## Record progress = commit (this is how progress is read)
271	
272	Your commits — message + diff — are the durable record of what you did; the
273	dashboard reads progress from them. Commit coherent progress yourself with plain
274	`git` into the workspace ledger. Skill: `project-git` (use `"$HORIZON_GIT" commit -m …`
275	or the explicit `--git-dir/--work-tree` form; provenance trailers are auto-stamped).
276	
277	Write **semantic, math-first** messages that say what you proved/built. Prefer
278	staging explicit files over `add -A`. Beyond commits:
279	
280	- Commit after each independently useful verified proof, file, or bounded tooling
281	  change; commit before long builds/reviews and before expanding scope. Multi-hour
282	  implementation sessions normally produce several commits.
283	- Never end a session with durable authored changes after the last commit. The
284	  lifecycle hook gives a compact checkpoint reminder and may pause Stop when it
285	  observed a file mutation after the last commit.
286	- Keep operational prose as a delta. Task/roadmap/inbox comments default to one
287	  sentence or at most three bullets: conclusion, evidence, next action. Do not
288	  copy the report, commit summary, or thread history into them.
289	
290	- Update the **roadmap** with coarse status/strategy (not a re-narration of the diff).
291	- Use the **inbox** to hand off to the next/other sessions; record durable dead-ends
292	  as **memory**.
293	
294	Before your final report, do one boundary-maintenance pass. Re-read the task's
295	`roadmap_refs` and `inbox_refs`; update each roadmap milestone whose status or
296	strategy changed, add a concise mathematical comment for a key advance, and
297	archive or complete open inbox items your work actually resolved. Also scan the
298	remaining open inbox for consumed temporary/info/memory items and archive those
299	that are now stale. Never archive a standing protection merely to make the list
300	shorter. In particular, review every open conversation your task started: archive
301	answered threads and leave a concrete blocker on any that must stay open. This
302	pass is part of completing the work, not optional janitor follow-up.
303	
304	## Resuming after an interruption
305	
306	State lives on disk, so a fresh session (even on another account) continues
307	cheaply. Working out *whether* you're resuming, and what to read if you are, is
308	the `horizon-start` skill — load it at the start of the session. The essentials:
309	
310	- **Why did the last run stop?** `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json` includes a
311	  `paused` field (from `runs/<id>/paused.json`) with the reason (usage limit,
312	  budget, …) and the exact resume command; `recent_failure_reasons` shows
313	  rate-limit signals. A paused/killed run resumes with
314	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" run --resume <id>`.
315	- **What was in flight?** Read recent ledger history (`project-git` skill:
316	  `git log` + `git show` by `Archon-Session` trailer) and the previous
317	  session's transcript/report under `.archon-horizon/runs/`. A horizon session
318	  directory with **no `report.md`** is one that was killed mid-flight.
319	- **Is another run live on this workspace?** `"$HORIZON_BIN" ps` lists runs
320	  holding a process (the ledger is one shared branch — be aware of parallel
321	  writers); it also flags zombie markers and stalled runs. A run registers a
322	  `runs/<id>/process.json` marker (pid/host) at start and removes it on clean
323	  exit; `ps` decides liveness by probing the pid on the local host (a marker whose
324	  pid is dead is a reap-able zombie, a live pid idle for a long time is "stalled").
325	  The synchronizer surfaces the same "other runs live" signal at command start, so
326	  you usually don't need to call `ps` explicitly.
327	
328	## Final report (your last message)
329	
330	Your final message is saved as the session's report — a human or the next
331	session should understand the session from it without opening raw logs.
332	Use only sections that carry information: normally `## Progress`, `## Issues`,
333	`## Why I stopped`, and `## Next`. In `## Progress`, use one inline `-` bullet per file/target,
334	e.g. `- FileA.lean: 4 sorries -> 3; closed the base case.` In `## Why I
335	stopped`, say plainly whether the objective is fully complete, partly advanced,
336	or blocked — and why. Always mention build failures, broken proofs, blocked
337	dependencies, and checks that failed or were not run. If a plausible next
338	action fits in the session's scope, take it before stopping — a clean commit is
339	not by itself a reason to stop. Do not replay the chronological session log.
340	
341	## Cleaning up the work (you decide, via subagents)
342	
343	There is no second orchestrator role running alongside you. *You* are the driver,
344	and the **`ground`** subagent is the scheduled fresh-context checkpoint when the
345	workspace or strategy needs an external view. Available helpers (see the
346	`subagents` skill):
347	
348	- **janitor** — workspace hygiene: roadmap/READMEs concise, inbox from overflowing.
349	- **ground** — workspace-wide strategy, graph, ledger, and convergence review.
350	- **work-reviewer** — fresh-context review of your last work; is it converging?
351	- **blueprint** — Lean ↔ blueprint statement/`\uses` correctness for a scoped slice.
352	- **reference-retriever**, **debug**, **page-transcriber** — as needed.
353	
354	Keep proving; delegate the upkeep.

2	name: lean-check
3	description: Build and check Lean in this workspace and read the errors — use Lean LSP MCP for fast proof-writing feedback, then run faithful kernel verification with `lake build` / `lake env lean`.
4	---
5	
6	## Required proof loop
7	
8	Load this skill before editing a Lean file. Before the first proof edit, invoke
9	at least one Lean LSP MCP query for the target (`lean_diagnostic_messages` or
10	`lean_goal`). After every proof edit, invoke diagnostics or the goal query again
11	before starting another tactic attempt. Use `lean_multi_attempt`, hover, and
12	search to investigate candidates instead of repeatedly launching a build.
13	
14	Do not start iterative proof work with `lake build`: it is a slow, final-boundary
15	check. Use LSP for the edit loop and reserve `lake build` for the final session
16	validation (or when a kernel check is specifically needed). When LSP is
17	unavailable or crashes, record that in the report and use the narrowest fallback,
18	usually `lake env lean <file>` or a single module, rather than silently skipping
19	the check.
20	
21	LSP is sufficient between edits and between separate obligations. Do not run a
22	module build after every proof or repeat a narrow build immediately before a
23	configured final build that covers the same files. At the final boundary, run
24	the configured build once and wait for it. Add an earlier narrow kernel check
25	only when LSP failed, the change crosses an interface LSP cannot validate, or a
26	specific elaboration/kernel question must be settled before continuing.
27	
28	- During proof writing, prefer the Lean LSP MCP server for fast local feedback:
29	  inspect goals/diagnostics at the edited location before running a full build.
30	  This is the fastest loop for filling proofs.
31	- Treat LSP feedback as interactive guidance, not final verification. The
32	  faithful check is Lean's kernel via the project build: run the configured
33	  build command, `lake build <Module>`, or `lake env lean <file>` from the
34	  project root.
35	- Prefer the project's configured build command when validating a task. Otherwise
36	  use the narrowest faithful check that covers the changed file/module.
37	- Re-run after each change and repair failures you introduce.
38	- Read errors top-down — the first error often causes the cascade. For each,
39	  note the `file:line`, expected vs actual type, and remaining goal.
40	- A `sorry` left in place is an open obligation, not a success. Do not hide a
41	  hard obligation behind a new `sorry` unless a hint explicitly allows it.
42	
43	## Fast LSP proving loop
44	
45	The `lean-lsp` MCP server gives sub-second feedback — far faster than a build
46	(10–30s+). Drive proofs with it, then confirm with the kernel. Key tools:
47	
48	- `lean_goal(file, line)` — the proof state at a line. Call before writing any
49	  tactic and after each one. Empty `goals_after` = that step closes the goal.
50	- `lean_diagnostic_messages(file)` — instant errors/warnings after every edit
51	  (`[]` = no errors, but *not* proof-complete — confirm with `lean_goal`).
52	- `lean_multi_attempt(file, line, snippets=[...])` — test 3–5 **single-line,
53	  indented** candidate tactics at once and see exactly which close the goal and
54	  why the others fail. The highest-leverage tool for filling a `sorry`.
55	- `lean_hover_info(file, line, col)` — type/signature/docs at an identifier
56	  (point at the first char). `lean_file_outline(file)` — declarations + line
57	  numbers without reading the whole file. `lean_run_code("#eval …")` — quick
58	  standalone `#check`/`#eval`/`#print`.
59	
60	Core loop: `lean_goal` (what to prove) → search a premise (see the `leansearch`
61	skill: `lean_local_search` / `lean_leansearch`) → `lean_multi_attempt` (test
62	candidates) → edit with the winner → `lean_diagnostic_messages` (confirm) →
63	kernel-check the module at the end.
64	
65	## Heavy builds — actually wait for them
66	
67	Read the WHOLE build output, not just pass/fail: warnings (unused variables,
68	deprecations, `sorry` notices, unexpected recompiles) are actionable — fix the
69	ones your change introduced, and record pre-existing/toolchain ones as memory
70	or an inbox issue rather than scrolling past (see the `horizon` skill,
71	"Warnings are work").
72	
73	A cold `lake build` (or one that recompiles Mathlib) can take many minutes. The
74	most common way a session ends on a wrong conclusion is **not waiting for the
75	build to finish**:
76	
77	- Do **not** assume you will be "automatically notified" or "re-invoked" when a
78	  background build completes — whether that happens depends entirely on the
79	  mechanism you used. If unsure, run the build in the **foreground** and block on
80	  it until it exits, then read the exit code.
81	- If you run it in the background, you MUST actively wait: poll its status/output
82	  until there is a definitive exit code (a monitor / until-loop, re-reading the
83	  log), and only then conclude. A background job you started but walked away from
84	  is *not* done.
85	- Scope the build to the narrowest faithful check (`lake build <Module>` or
86	  `lake env lean <file>`) to keep the wait short; reserve the full project build
87	  for final validation.
88	- Never write your final report — or `complete` an inbox item, or mark a task
89	  done — while a build that affects your conclusion is still running. If the
90	  engine cannot wait long enough, say so explicitly under `## Issues` and leave
91	  the next action clear, rather than implying the proof checked.
92	- Before marking a task or roadmap item done/blocked/rejected, add a concise
93	  closing comment with the exact check command, result, relevant files, and any
94	  caveat. If a task has `roadmap_refs`, make sure the linked roadmap items end
95	  with a consistent status and their own sync/closing comment.
96	
97	## When the LSP dies on big import files
98	
99	The Lean LSP loads the full environment for the file you open. On a file whose
100	imports pull in most of Mathlib (a broad `import Mathlib` umbrella, or a module
101	that transitively imports one), that environment is huge and the LSP server can
102	run out of memory or time out and die. This is an LSP limitation, **not** a
103	proof error:
104	
105	- Do not treat an LSP crash/timeout on such a file as a failure of your proof.
106	  Fall back to the kernel check: `lake build <Module>` or `lake env lean <file>`,
107	  which verifies faithfully without holding the whole environment interactively.
108	- Prefer opening the **narrowest** module in the LSP. Avoid pointing the LSP at
109	  umbrella/`import Mathlib`-style files just to get feedback; edit and inspect
110	  the specific module you are proving in instead.
111	- If the LSP has crashed, restart it (or just proceed with `lake build`) rather
112	  than repeatedly reopening the same giant file and getting the same crash.

2	name: project-git
3	description: How git works in an Archon Horizon workspace — one out-of-tree workspace ledger (no per-project repos); read a project's history by pathspec or by a session's commit trailers.
4	---
5	
6	Read this before running `git diff`/`git log` on a project.
7	
8	## The model
9	
10	- **One out-of-tree workspace ledger.** Archon commits to a single repo whose git
11	  dir is `.archon-horizon/vcs/workspace.git` with the workspace **root** as its
12	  work tree (driven via `--git-dir`/`--work-tree`). `<root>/.git` is deliberately
13	  untouched — it is reserved for a user repo. The ledger records one commit per
14	  completed session: `config.yaml`, the session's scoped project files, and
15	  `.archon-horizon/` shared state; never the binary git dirs under
16	  `.archon-horizon/vcs/`, locks, or other volatile internals.
17	- **There are no per-project repositories.** A project directory has no nested
18	  `.git/`, and there is no `.archon-horizon/vcs/<project>.git`. A project's
19	  "history" is simply the workspace ledger filtered to that project's path.
20	- **You record your own work by committing to the ledger** with plain `git` (see
21	  below). Commit after each independently useful, verified proof/file/tooling
22	  change, before a long build or delegated review, and before expanding scope.
23	  A multi-hour implementation session should normally have several commits; one
24	  commit is appropriate only when the work is genuinely atomic. The message +
25	  diff is how progress is read, so use a semantic, math-first subject. Provenance
26	  trailers are added automatically; do not write them.
27	
28	So a plain `git diff` at the root sees only a user repo (if any), never Archon's.
29	Drive the out-of-tree workspace ledger explicitly (or use `hgit`).
30	
31	## Recording your work (committing)
32	
33	Commits go to the ledger, **not** to `<root>/.git` and **not** via any project
34	`.git` (there is none). Do **not** `export GIT_DIR` / `GIT_WORK_TREE` yourself — that
35	would redirect `lake` and other tooling. Two equivalent ways to commit:
36	
37	```bash
38	# 1) The `hgit` wrapper (on the session env as $HORIZON_GIT) — plain git, ledger-scoped:
39	"$HORIZON_GIT" add path/to/File.lean
40	"$HORIZON_GIT" commit -m "feat(chapter): prove foo_lemma" \
41	  --trailer 'Summary=**Proof.** Closed the compactness step using $K \subseteq X$.'
42	
43	# 2) The explicit form (identical effect):
44	git --git-dir="$HORIZON_LEDGER_GIT_DIR" --work-tree="$HORIZON_LEDGER_WORK_TREE" \
45	    add path/to/File.lean
46	git --git-dir="$HORIZON_LEDGER_GIT_DIR" --work-tree="$HORIZON_LEDGER_WORK_TREE" \
47	    commit -m "feat(chapter): prove foo_lemma" \
48	    --trailer 'Summary=**Proof.** Closed the compactness step using $K \subseteq X$.'
49	```
50	
51	Ordinary git: the ledger's index tracks HEAD, so `add` then `commit` records your
52	files on top of it. Horizon's own commits stage in a private index and never leave
53	anything staged in your way.
54	
55	- **Prefer the pathspec commit** — name the paths on the commit itself:
56	  `"$HORIZON_GIT" commit -m "…" --trailer 'Summary=…' -- path/to/File.lean`
57	  It records exactly those files, ignores whatever else may be staged, and git
58	  builds its tree from the **current** HEAD — so it cannot silently revert a
59	  concurrent session's files the way a commit built on a stale index can.
60	- Add at least one **`Summary` trailer** explaining the important change, not
61	  merely repeating the subject. Use one trailer per distinct explanation when
62	  useful. Its value supports Markdown and LaTeX, so concise mathematical context
63	  such as `--trailer 'Summary=**Invariant.** Preserves $f(x)=x$ on $A$.'` renders
64	  directly in the dashboard commit item. Keep each trailer on one line; repeat
65	  `--trailer 'Summary=…'` for a few separate points.
66	- Do not wait for the whole task to be complete. A checkpoint commit must build
67	  or otherwise be internally coherent, but it may explicitly leave the next
68	  named obligation open.
69	- Stage **explicit paths** you changed rather than `add -A` — the work tree is the
70	  whole workspace, so `-A` can sweep in unrelated files.
71	- `Archon-Run`/`Session`/`Role`/`Task`/`Projects` trailers are stamped for you by a
72	  hook from the session env; your message stays clean.
73	- Build artifacts (`.lake`, `*.olean`, …) are excluded automatically, and any
74	  high-confidence credential is **redacted to `XXXX`** in the staged content (not
75	  blocked), so a broad add still won't leak a secret into the ledger.
76	- If the guard reports *"redacted possible secret(s) to XXXX"*, it scrubbed a
77	  matched credential and let the commit through — **rotate the real credential**,
78	  and check you didn't stage more than you meant to (`ARCHON_HORIZON_ALLOW_SECRETS=1`
79	  skips the scan entirely). A *separate* guard still **blocks** a commit that would
80	  silently delete tracked files you didn't change (a stale-index clobber); re-seed
81	  the index (`git read-tree HEAD && git add -- <your files>`) rather than forcing it.
82	
83	Then verify **in the ledger**, and verify the **paths**, not just the SHA — a bare
84	`git cat-file` runs against `<root>/.git`, which has not seen your commit yet and will
85	make a perfectly real SHA look fabricated:
86	
87	```bash
88	"$HORIZON_GIT" ls-tree --name-only HEAD -- path/to/File.lean   # empty ⇒ NOT in HEAD
89	```
90	
91	## Concurrent sessions and the clobber guard
92	
93	Several sessions may commit to the ledger at once. A commit whose index was
94	seeded from an older HEAD (e.g. `read-tree`, then a concurrent session commits,
95	then you commit) produces a tree that *lacks* the other session's new files —
96	plain git would commit it without any error and silently delete their work.
97	The ledger's `pre-commit` guard now rejects any commit that stages deletions
98	you did not ask for:
99	
100	- *"this commit would DELETE N tracked file(s) you did not change"* — your
101	  index base is stale (or you are committing through a polluted shared index).
102	  **Do not override.** Re-seed and retry; your own edits are safe in the
103	  working tree, which concurrent commits never touch:
104	
105	  ```bash
106	  "$HORIZON_GIT" read-tree HEAD
107	  "$HORIZON_GIT" add -- <your files>
108	  "$HORIZON_GIT" commit -m "…"          # or just: commit -m "…" -- <your files>
109	  ```
110	
111	- Deleting a file **on purpose** (moved/retired): set
112	  `ARCHON_HORIZON_ALLOW_DELETIONS=1` for that one commit.
113	
114	At the **end of the session**, re-verify content — not just that HEAD moved —
115	since a stale-based commit elsewhere could have landed after yours (the guard
116	blocks new offenders, but belt-and-braces):
117	
118	```bash
119	"$HORIZON_GIT" cat-file -e HEAD:path/to/File.lean && \
120	"$HORIZON_GIT" show HEAD:path/to/File.lean | diff -q - path/to/File.lean
121	```
122	
123	If you were clobbered anyway: `read-tree HEAD`, re-add your files from the
124	working tree, commit once.
125	
126	## Reading history / a project's diff
127	
128	Run from the workspace root:
129	
130	```bash
131	GD=.archon-horizon/vcs/workspace.git
132	
133	git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. log  --oneline -n 20                       # whole ledger
134	git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. log  --oneline -n 20 -- <project-path>     # one project
135	git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. diff HEAD~1 -- <project-path>
136	git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. diff HEAD~1 -- '<project-path>/*.lean'
137	git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. show <sha>
138	```
139	
140	Each commit carries provenance trailers — `Archon-Run`, `Archon-Session`,
141	`Archon-Role`, `Archon-Task`, `Archon-Projects` — so you can map a commit to the
142	run/session that made it and see what it touched without parsing prose:
143	
144	```bash
145	git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. \
146	  log --format='%H %(trailers:key=Archon-Session,valueonly)' -- <project-path>
147	```
148	
149	To see what the previous Horizon agent changed, find its session's commit(s) by
150	the `Archon-Session` trailer and diff each against **its own parent** (what that
151	commit changed).
152	
153	## Caveats
154	
155	- With parallel runs the ledger is one shared branch: commits from several runs
156	  interleave, and a commit's parent may belong to another run or a dashboard
157	  publish. Diff a commit against its own parent (what *that* commit changed), not
158	  across a span of sessions — that would fold in unrelated runs' changes.
159	- The bundled author identity is `Archon Horizon <archon-horizon@local>`.
160

/-!
# `hcpt` IS NOT A FIFTH OBLIGATION: the atlas's compactness input is the qc field's own hypothesis

`Picard/Pic0AtlasFiniteType.lean` corrected the board's three-antecedent picture of the
distance to representability to **four**, discharged the fourth (`hlft`), and then named the
input its own assembly leaves exposed:

> `hcpt` — `CompactSpace` of the glued object.  **Open**, and it is the input this file leaves
> exposed. […] the two routes the tree already names are still the honest ones: a finite
> atlas, or the Abel image.

That dichotomy is **incomplete**, and this file is the correction.  There is a third route, it
was already on the board under a different row (`dat-j.qcfield`), and it needs nothing the
assembly does not already have:

  `compactSpace_of_pic0_class_surjective` (`Picard/JacobianDataQcFromRep.lean`) applied to the
  atlas's *own* representation `pic0RepresentableByOfCharts C (mixedParamChart …) hf` yields
  `CompactSpace (Scheme.LocalRepresentability.glueData hf).glued` — which is the `hcpt` slot of
  `jacobianDataOfMixedParamCharts` **on the nose**
  (`gluedOfCharts_left_eq_glued`, `rfl`).

## What this changes, precisely

The assembly's input list goes from five to four, and the fifth is not *removed* — it is
identified with one already there:

| input of `jacobianDataOfMixedParamCharts` | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `rep` (divisor representability) | open | open, unchanged |
| `hf` (`IsChartUniv`) | open | open, unchanged |
| the `IsLocallySurjective` instance (coverage) | open | open, unchanged |
| `hD` (`LocallyOfFiniteType (D i).hom`) | discharged | discharged, unchanged |
| **`hcpt` (`CompactSpace` of the glued)** | **open, "the exposed one"** | **implied by `hcl`** |

`hcl` is the class-coordinate lift hypothesis of the `dat-j.qcfield` row: *every point of the
representing object has its class pulled back from a fixed degree-zero class `lam` on the
divisor scheme along some field point.*  So a lane discharging the qc field discharges `hcpt`

14	`DivisorAdaptation` (pieces typed into a fixed pair of pinned `P¹` charts) to `AffAdaptation`
15	(arbitrary affine opens, human decision I-0492).  The port is **complete**: the widened

17	nothing in the chain remains conditional on the chart typing.

20	
21	The board carried this as a **four**-lemma port.  It is five: the prescription omitted
22	`coeffAt_eq_toAdd_ordZ_eqn`, the coefficient dictionary that both other geometric lemmas call.
23	That is the only way the estimate was wrong, and it was wrong in the cheap direction — not one
24	proof step of any of the five differs from its chart-typed original.

30	  piece is a basic open of a pinned affine chart; `AffCoverData.isAffineOpen_pieces` is the field.

32	  (`RiemannRoch/ChartColength.lean`, in `AlgebraicGeometry` with no further namespace), takes
33	  `IsAffineOpen V` as an *argument* — it never wanted a chart.

10	# The colength↔degree identity for divisor families over a field (`informal/spec-dd-1.md` §3 (f))
11	
12	Over a field `K` the forward map `divFamDivisor` (`AlgebraicJacobian.Picard.DivisorFamilyField`)
13	sends a certified divisor family to its Weil divisor. This file lands the **degree identity**
14	
15	`deg K (divFamDivisor F) = finrank K W(d)`
16	
17	(so, with the field half `DivisorAdaptation.IsCertified.finrank_glued`, `deg = n`), the
18	colength↔degree bridge across the glued equalizer `W(d) = ker (δ⁻ − δ⁺)`.
19	
20	## The support-separated assembly
21	
22	The equalizer does not decompose over the cover naively — a supported closed point may lie in
23	two pieces. This file proves the **support-separated** case, which is the one the DD-1c backward
24	map consumes (its adaptations isolate the support points by construction): when the overlap
25	colength modules vanish (`ovlColength i j` is subsingleton for `i ≠ j`), the equalizer is the
26	*whole* product of the chart-local colengths, so
27	
28	`finrank K W(d) = ∑ⱼ finrank K (Γ(D(hⱼ)) ⧸ (fⱼ))`  (`finrank_glued_eq_sum_of_separated`),
29	
30	pure module algebra (`Module.finrank_pi_fintype` over the field, where every factor is free).
31	-/

56	when the order of `g` at `z` is trivial (`ordZ = 1`). -/

67	      = (stalkHeightOne X z).valuation X.functionField := rfl
68	  have hgs : (X.presheaf.germ U (genericPoint X) hη).hom f
69	      = algebraMap (X.presheaf.stalk z) X.functionField
70	          ((X.presheaf.germ U z hz).hom f) := by

72	    exact (X.presheaf.germ_stalkSpecializes_apply hz

154	  · rintro t ⟨s, hs, rfl⟩
155	    exact (A.mem_gluedSubmodule_chartProdCongr_iff s).mpr hs
156	
157	/-- **The glued modules are equivalent** — the map along which (c2)/(c3)/(c4) transport. -/
158	noncomputable def gluedCongr : A.Glued ≃ₗ[R] A.toAff.Glued :=
159	  (A.chartProdCongr.submoduleMap A.gluedSubmodule).trans
160	    (LinearEquiv.ofEq _ _ A.gluedSubmodule_toAff.symm)
161	
162	/-- **(c3) transports**: the inclusion cokernels are equivalent, `chartProdCongr` carrying
163	`gluedSubmodule` onto `gluedSubmodule`. -/
164	noncomputable def cokerInclCongr :
165	    (A.chartProd ⧸ A.gluedSubmodule) ≃ₗ[R] (A.toAff.chartProd ⧸ A.toAff.gluedSubmodule) :=
166	  Submodule.Quotient.equiv _ _ A.chartProdCongr A.gluedSubmodule_toAff.symm
167	
168	/-- **(c4) transports**: the difference-arrow ranges correspond under `ovlProdCongr`. -/
169	lemma difference_square :
170	    (A.toAff.deltaLeft - A.toAff.deltaRight) ∘ₗ (A.chartProdCongr : A.chartProd →ₗ[R] _)
171	      = (A.ovlProdCongr : A.ovlProd →ₗ[R] _) ∘ₗ (A.deltaLeft - A.deltaRight) := by
172	  refine LinearMap.ext fun s => ?_
173	  have hL := (A.ovlProdCongr : A.ovlProd →ₗ[R] A.toAff.ovlProd).map_sub
174	    (A.deltaLeft s) (A.deltaRight s)
175	  change A.toAff.deltaLeft (A.chartProdCongr s) - A.toAff.deltaRight (A.chartProdCongr s)
176	      = (A.ovlProdCongr : A.ovlProd →ₗ[R] A.toAff.ovlProd) ((A.deltaLeft - A.deltaRight) s)
177	  rw [LinearMap.sub_apply, hL, A.deltaLeft_chartProdCongr, A.deltaRight_chartProdCongr]
178	  rfl
179	
180	lemma range_sub_toAff :
181	    LinearMap.range (A.toAff.deltaLeft - A.toAff.deltaRight)
182	      = Submodule.map (A.ovlProdCongr : A.ovlProd →ₗ[R] _)
183	          (LinearMap.range (A.deltaLeft - A.deltaRight)) := by
184	  have h1 : LinearMap.range ((A.toAff.deltaLeft - A.toAff.deltaRight)
185	        ∘ₗ (A.chartProdCongr : A.chartProd →ₗ[R] A.toAff.chartProd))
186	      = LinearMap.range (A.toAff.deltaLeft - A.toAff.deltaRight) :=
187	    LinearMap.range_comp_of_range_eq_top _
188	      (LinearMap.range_eq_top.mpr A.chartProdCongr.surjective)
189	  rw [← h1, A.difference_square, LinearMap.range_comp]
190	
191	/-- The difference cokernels are equivalent. -/
192	noncomputable def cokerDiffCongr :
193	    (A.ovlProd ⧸ LinearMap.range (A.deltaLeft - A.deltaRight)) ≃ₗ[R]
194	      (A.toAff.ovlProd ⧸ LinearMap.range (A.toAff.deltaLeft - A.toAff.deltaRight)) :=
195	  Submodule.Quotient.equiv _ _ A.ovlProdCongr A.range_sub_toAff.symm
196	
197	/-- **The certificate migrates, all seven clauses.**  Clauses (c1) are `rfl` at the
198	relabelled index; (c2)/(c3)/(c4) transport along `gluedCongr`, `cokerInclCongr` and
199	`cokerDiffCongr`.  Nothing is weakened and nothing is re-proved — this is what makes
200	"consumers port by reindexing alone" a theorem rather than a hope. -/
201	theorem isCertified_toAff {n : ℕ} (hA : A.IsCertified n) : A.toAff.IsCertified n where
202	  finite_colength := fun j => hA.finite_colength (A.reindexEquiv j)
203	  projective_colength := fun j => hA.projective_colength (A.reindexEquiv j)
204	  finite_glued :=
205	    haveI := hA.finite_glued
206	    Module.Finite.equiv A.gluedCongr
207	  projective_glued :=
208	    haveI := hA.projective_glued
209	    Module.Projective.of_equiv A.gluedCongr
210	  rankAtStalk_glued := fun p => by
211	    rw [← Module.rankAtStalk_eq_of_equiv A.gluedCongr]
212	    exact hA.rankAtStalk_glued p
213	  flat_coker_incl :=
214	    haveI := hA.flat_coker_incl
215	    Module.Flat.of_linearEquiv A.cokerInclCongr.symm
216	  flat_coker_diff :=
217	    haveI := hA.flat_coker_diff
218	    Module.Flat.of_linearEquiv A.cokerDiffCongr.symm
219	
220	end DivisorAdaptation
